title: Consistent Hashing — distribute data across nodes so adding/removing a node moves only K/N keys (not all), used in distributed caches and databases.

s1_definition.profdef: Consistent hashing is a distribution technique that maps both data keys and server nodes onto a conceptual ring using a hash function, assigning each key to the first node clockwise from it. Its defining property is that adding or removing a node remaps only about one over the number of nodes of the keys, rather than nearly all keys as naive modulo hashing would. Virtual nodes are used to smooth out uneven key distribution and load.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose National Bank of India stores customer records across several branches by taking the account number modulo the branch count. If one branch opens or closes, the count changes, and suddenly almost every customer's record maps to a different branch, forcing a massive, chaotic migration. Consistent hashing is a smarter scheme: picture a clock face with branches placed around it, and each customer placed on the clock too, assigned to the next branch clockwise. If one branch closes, only the customers between it and the previous branch move; everyone else stays put.
s1_definition.oneliner: Place nodes and keys on a hash ring and assign each key to the next node clockwise, so adding or removing a node moves only a small slice of keys, not all of them.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Consistent hashing is a distribution technique that maps both data keys and server nodes onto a conceptual ring using a hash function, assigning each key to the first node clockwise from it. Its defining property is that adding or removing a node remaps only about one over the number of nodes of the keys, rather than nearly all keys as naive modulo hashing would. Virtual nodes are used to smooth out uneven key distribution and load.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose National Bank of India stores customer records across several branches by taking the account number modulo the branch count. If one branch opens or closes, the count changes, and suddenly almost every customer's record maps to a different branch, forcing a massive, chaotic migration. Consistent hashing is a smarter scheme: picture a clock face with branches placed around it, and each customer placed on the clock too, assigned to the next branch clockwise. If one branch closes, only the customers between it and the previous branch move; everyone else stays put.

**One line to remember:** Place nodes and keys on a hash ring and assign each key to the next node clockwise, so adding or removing a node moves only a small slice of keys, not all of them.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India caches customer balances across several cache nodes using account number modulo node count, and when it added a node during growth, almost every balance remapped and the cache emptied, causing a storm of database reads. The real problem is massive remapping on scale. This is exactly what consistent hashing prevents.

Problem 2 — a cache node failed, and the bank needed only that node's keys to move, not a full reshuffle. The real problem is minimal movement on node loss. This is exactly what the ring's clockwise ownership provides.

Problem 3 — with only three nodes, one node ended up holding most of the keys. The real problem is uneven distribution. This is exactly what virtual nodes smooth out.

We build a runnable `ConsistentHashRing` with virtual nodes, showing which node owns each key, how adding a node moves only a small fraction of keys, and how removing a node moves only its keys. The demo places customer balance keys, adds and removes a node, and counts how many keys actually moved versus a naive modulo scheme.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is one thousand balance keys and a ring with one hundred virtual nodes per physical node, starting with three nodes.

Step 1: Each key is hashed onto the ring and assigned to the first node clockwise, spreading the thousand keys roughly evenly across the three nodes thanks to virtual nodes. This ownership is recorded as the before state.

Step 2: A fourth node is added. Only keys that now fall into the arcs the new node covers are reassigned to it; the rest keep their previous owner. Counting the differences shows roughly a quarter of the keys moved, which is about one over four, the expected fraction.

Step 3: For contrast, the naive modulo scheme is computed for three and four nodes, and nearly all keys differ between them because changing the divisor changes almost every result. This dramatizes why modulo hashing is unstable.

Step 4: A node is removed, and only the keys that node owned move to the next node clockwise, which is again a small share rather than a full reshuffle. The data that changed is only the ownership of the minimal set of affected keys.

```
2026-11-01 01:30:00 [INFO] Consistent hashing: 247/1000 keys moved on add (~K/N)
2026-11-01 01:30:00 [INFO] Naive modulo: 743/1000 keys moved on add (nearly all)
2026-11-01 01:30:00 [INFO] On removing cache-B: 251/1000 keys moved (only its share)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  1000 keys hashed onto the ring (3 nodes, 100 vnodes each)
    │ each key → first node clockwise
    ▼
  balanced ownership (A, B, C hold ~1/3 each)

  ADD cache-D
    │ only arcs now covered by D are reassigned
    ▼
  ~250/1000 keys move to D; rest UNTOUCHED  ← K/N property

  (contrast) NAIVE MODULO 3 → 4
    │ hash(key) % N changes for almost every key
    ▼
  ~750/1000 keys move  ← disruptive

  REMOVE cache-B
    │ only B's keys go to next node clockwise
    ▼
  ~250/1000 keys move; A, C, D keep their keys
```

```
  ═══ LLD — Consistent Hash Ring ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Ring via TreeMap ceilingEntry = clockwise successor      │

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │     ConsistentHashRing       │
  │ - ring: TreeMap<Int,String>  │
  │ - vnodes: int                │
  │ + addNode(node)              │
  │ + removeNode(node)           │
  │ + nodeFor(key): String       │
  │ - hash(s): int               │
  └──────────────────────────────┘
          contrast
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │     NaiveModuloHashing       │
  │ - nodeCount                  │
  │ + nodeFor(key): int          │  ← remaps almost all on change
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  ── Behavior (as state) ────────────────────────────────────

  [STABLE] ──add node──→ [REBALANCING ~K/N] ──done──→ [STABLE]
  [STABLE] ──remove node──→ [REBALANCING node's keys] ──done──→ [STABLE]

  ── Call Chain (nodeFor) ───────────────────────────────────

  1. nodeFor("balance:ACC42")
  2.   → h = hash(key)
  3.   → ring.ceilingEntry(h)  (first node clockwise)
  4.   → wrap to firstEntry if past the end
  5.   → return node

  Contract for nodeFor(key):
    Pre:  ring non-empty
    Post: returns owning node; stable unless an arc's node changes
    Invariant: add/remove moves ~K/N keys, not all
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Consistent hashing is a distribution technique that maps both data keys and server nodes onto a conceptual ring and assigns each key to the first node clockwise from it. Its defining property, and the reason it exists, is that adding or removing a node moves only about one over the number of nodes of the keys, instead of nearly all of them as naive modulo hashing would. That minimal-movement property is what makes it the backbone of distributed caches and databases.

The problem it solves is the instability of modulo hashing. If I place a key on the node equal to the hash of the key modulo the node count, then changing the node count changes the result for almost every key. In a distributed cache that means a near-total cache-miss storm every time I scale, and in a database it means moving almost all the data. At National Bank of India, exactly this happened: we cached balances with account number modulo node count, and adding a node during growth remapped nearly every balance, emptied the cache, and triggered a storm of database reads.

Consistent hashing fixes this by hashing each node to one or more points on a ring and each key to a point, with a key owned by the first node clockwise from it. When I add a node, it takes over only the keys in the arcs between it and its predecessors, and all other keys keep their owner. When I remove a node, only its keys move to the next node clockwise. In the demo, adding a fourth node moved roughly a quarter of a thousand keys, while naive modulo moved nearly three quarters, which makes the difference concrete.

The practical refinement I always mention is virtual nodes. With only a few physical nodes the ring can be unevenly divided, so one node ends up holding most of the keys. Placing each physical node at many points on the ring finely interleaves the arcs and balances load, and weighting the number of virtual points lets stronger hardware carry proportionally more. Consistent hashing also enables replication by walking clockwise to the next N distinct nodes, which is exactly how systems like Cassandra and DynamoDB place replicas. That combination of minimal key movement, virtual-node balancing, and clockwise replication is why consistent hashing is the standard way to distribute data across a changing set of nodes.
